nurse_note:
Case ID: HOLD-HTN-01

The driver brought a torn home-pressure diary. Three entries from the past week are around 176/102, but the dates on two lines are incomplete and the clinic obtained only one seated reading today after the driver rushed in from the car park. He says the tablets were restarted recently and asks if the lower reading remembered from last year cancels the diary. The nurse records possible sustained elevation but cannot verify the series or use last year's figure as today's pressure.

Case ID: HOLD-HTN-02

At follow-up, the driver says his repeated pressures have improved since antihypertensive treatment, yet the dose was changed three weeks ago and he has briefly felt faint when standing at the depot. The referral does not document a completed period of stable control, whether the dizziness impairs driving, or a specialist review of relevant organ damage. A colleague's comment that he looks well is recorded as hearsay rather than clearance.

Case ID: HOLD-VIS-01

During night deliveries the driver sometimes sees a second image beside an oncoming vehicle. Closing either eye removes the doubling, but he was symptom-free during this morning's appointment. A routine chart reading was recorded without noting whether glasses were worn, and no examiner measured the position of the double image relative to straight-ahead vision. The nurse does not treat a normal office conversation as proof that the driving symptom has resolved.

Case ID: HOLD-VIS-02

The driver reports missing cyclists entering from one side. An old printout says 138 degrees across both eyes, while a recent automated field result carries a low-reliability warning and does not state whether the central area was clear. Neither paper confirms a stable defect or the full testing protocol. The nurse asks for a reliable binocular field assessment before treating either number as a current commercial-driving result.

nurse_note:
Case ID: HOLD-HEAR-01

The driver follows face-to-face speech while wearing hearing aids but misses radio calls in a running vehicle. A phone image of an audiogram shows some thresholds, although the ear labels and the 3000 Hz row are cut off. It is unclear whether the aids were in place during testing. The nurse cannot calculate an unaided better-ear average from the photograph and requests the signed audiology record.

Case ID: HOLD-HEAR-02

A signed audiology summary reports an average loss of exactly 40 dB in the better ear without hearing aids, using 500, 1000, 2000 and 3000 Hz. The driver says an earlier workplace screen had passed him, but that screen did not record the frequencies or better-ear calculation. The assessment needs the commercial threshold and any route involving hearing assistance, with the exact boundary preserved rather than rounded.

Case ID: HOLD-BLK-01

After an unresponsive spell at a loading bay, the driver remembers sitting down but not a coworker calling his name. The witness is unsure whether there were two episodes or one prolonged episode. An ECG has been arranged and a neurology referral remains open; neither clinician has established a mechanism. The nurse records the possibility of transient loss of awareness without assigning it to a cardiac, neurological or metabolic diagnosis.

nurse_note:
Case ID: HOLD-BLK-02

The driver became faint during a blood draw and recovered quickly after lying down. He calls it a harmless needle reaction, but the nurse has only his account; a separate unwitnessed spell at home is also mentioned in an old referral. The assessment needs to distinguish a clearly provoked faint from an event of uncertain nature before applying a return-to-driving interval.

nurse_note:
Case ID: HOLD-DM-01

The driver used to manage diabetes with food choices alone, but a current prescription list now includes a nightly insulin injection. He has brought a few meter screenshots rather than a continuous monitoring record and cannot remember the last specialist appointment. The nurse separates the current injected treatment from the historical diet-only description and requests the information needed for commercial-driver review.

nurse_note:
Case ID: HOLD-DM-02

A driver taking glucose-lowering medication became confused after a missed meal and a coworker gave him a sugary drink because he could not respond to the meter alarm. No glucose reading was captured until after treatment, and there is no clinician's account of the episode. He denies losing consciousness. The nurse records the assistance and uncertainty separately, then asks for assessment of severe hypoglycaemia and the related commercial-driving restrictions.
